title: Backspace string compare
prompt:
PageTurn's input log records each keystroke a student types, with # meaning backspace. A backspace deletes the most recent remaining character; a backspace on empty text does nothing.

Write sameFinalText(logA, logB) that returns true if the two logs produce the same final text.

Examples:

  • sameFinalText("cat#r", "cax#r") → true (both become "car")
  • sameFinalText("ab##", "c#d#") → true (both become "")
  • sameFinalText("a#c", "b") → false ("c" vs "b")

Constraints: 0 ≤ length of each log ≤ 200; logs contain lowercase letters and #.

tests.name: backspace on empty text does nothing
backspaces deep in the log

hints: A backspace undoes the most recent character: that's the undo shape of a stack.
Write a helper finalText(log): push each letter onto an array; on #, pop if the array isn't empty. Join the array. Then compare the two final texts.

Shape:

function finalText(log) {
  const typed = [];
  for (const ch of log) {
    if (ch === '#') { if (typed.length > 0) typed.pop(); }
    else typed.push(ch);
  }
  return typed.join('');
}
explain:
Time O(n + m), space O(n + m) for logs of length n and m. Each character is pushed and popped at most once. Deleting characters one at a time by rebuilding the string is O(n²).

Follow-up an interviewer may ask: do it in O(1) extra space. Walk both logs backward with two pointers, keeping a count of pending backspaces; skip characters that a later # cancels, then compare the next real characters. Same O(n + m) time, no arrays.

In an interview: "A backspace cancels the most recent character, so I'll build each final string with a stack: push letters, pop on #. That's O(n + m) time and space. If memory matters, I can walk both strings backward with two pointers for O(1) space."
